subject: Physics
experiment_name: Vernier Caliper Measurements
objective: To measure the external diameter, internal diameter, and depth of a given object using a vernier caliper.
theory: A vernier caliper is a precision measuring instrument used to measure lengths with higher accuracy than a standard scale. It consists of a main scale and a vernier scale. The vernier scale slides over the main scale and helps in measuring fractional parts of the smallest division of the main scale.
formula: Least Count (LC) = Value of one main scale division / Number of vernier scale divisions
Final Reading = Main Scale Reading (MSR) + (Vernier Scale Reading (VSR) × LC)
procedure: Clean the measuring jaws of the vernier caliper using a cloth.
Close the jaws completely and check for zero error.
Place the object between the appropriate jaws (external, internal, or depth rod).
Gently tighten the jaws so that they just touch the object.
Note the main scale reading (MSR) just before the zero of the vernier scale.
Identify the vernier division that coincides exactly with a main scale division.
Calculate the vernier scale reading (VSR).
Compute the final reading using the given formula.
calculations: Calculate least count using the formula: LC = MSD / Number of vernier divisions
Find final reading using: Final Reading = MSR + (VSR × LC)
precautions: Ensure the instrument is clean before use.
Check and correct zero error if present.
Avoid applying excessive pressure while measuring.
Take readings at eye level to avoid parallax error.
learning_outcome: Students learn how to use precision measuring instruments and understand the importance of least count and error minimization in measurements.

subject: Physics
experiment_name: Screw Gauge Measurement of Diameter of a Wire
objective: To measure the diameter of a given thin cylindrical wire using a screw gauge and determine its average value accurately.
theory: A screw gauge is a precision instrument used to measure very small dimensions accurately. It works on the principle of conversion of rotational motion into linear motion. When the thimble is rotated, the spindle moves forward or backward. The least count of a screw gauge is given by the ratio of pitch to the number of divisions on the circular scale. The total reading is obtained by adding the main scale reading and the circular scale reading multiplied by the least count, after applying zero correction if present.
formula: Least Count (LC) = Pitch / Number of divisions on circular scale
Observed Reading = Main Scale Reading + (Circular Scale Reading × LC)
Corrected Reading = Observed Reading ± Zero Error
procedure: Find the pitch of the screw gauge by rotating the thimble and noting the distance moved.
Determine the least count of the screw gauge.
Check for zero error by closing the jaws gently and note it.
Place the wire between the anvil and spindle.
Rotate the thimble gently until the wire is held properly without applying extra force.
Note the main scale reading and circular scale reading.
Repeat the measurement at different points along the wire to avoid irregularities.
Record at least 5 readings.
Apply zero correction to each reading.
Calculate the average diameter of the wire.
calculations: Calculate least count of the screw gauge.
Apply zero correction to all observed readings.
Determine diameter for each reading.
Find the mean (average) diameter of the wire.
precautions: Ensure the screw gauge is clean before use.
Do not apply excessive force while tightening the spindle.
Check and correct zero error before taking readings.
Take readings at different points of the wire.
Avoid parallax error while noting readings.
learning_outcome: To understand the working of a screw gauge and accurately measure the diameter of a thin wire using precise measurement techniques.

subject: Physics
experiment_name: Study of Simple Pendulum and Determination of Effective Length using L–T Graph
objective: To study the motion of a simple pendulum, understand energy conversion during oscillations, and draw the L–T graph to determine the effective length of a second pendulum.
theory: A simple pendulum consists of a small heavy bob suspended by a light inextensible string. When displaced from its mean position and released, it oscillates with simple harmonic motion for small angles. During motion, energy continuously converts between potential energy (maximum at extreme positions) and kinetic energy (maximum at mean position). The time period of a simple pendulum is given by T = 2π√(L/g), where L is the effective length. A graph between length (L) and square of time period (T²) is a straight line, which helps in determining unknown length.
procedure: Suspend the bob using a light string from a rigid support.
Measure the length of the pendulum from point of suspension to the center of the bob.
Displace the bob slightly and release it without giving any push.
Measure time for 10 oscillations using a stopwatch and calculate time period (T).
Repeat for different lengths and record readings.
Plot a graph between L and T².
From the graph, determine the effective length corresponding to the given time period of second pendulum.
calculations: Calculate time period T = total time / number of oscillations.
Find T² for each reading.
Plot L vs T² graph.
Determine slope and use it to find effective length.
precautions: Keep angular displacement small (less than 10°).
Avoid air currents and disturbances.
Release the bob gently without applying force.
Measure length accurately from suspension point to center of bob.
Use consistent number of oscillations for timing.
sources_of_error: Error in measuring length of pendulum.
Human reaction time error in stopwatch.
Air resistance and friction at pivot.
learning_outcome: To understand oscillatory motion, observe energy conversion between kinetic and potential energy, and use graphical methods to determine effective length.

subject: Physics
experiment_name: To Study the Relationship Between Marginal Force of Friction and Normal Reaction
objective: To study the relationship between marginal force of friction and normal reaction and to determine the coefficient of friction between a given block and a horizontal surface.
theory: Friction is the force that opposes the relative motion between two surfaces in contact. The limiting or marginal force of friction is the maximum value of static friction just before motion begins. It is directly proportional to the normal reaction between the surfaces. This relation is given by F ∝ R or F = μR, where μ is the coefficient of friction. The value of μ depends on the nature of the surfaces in contact.
procedure: Place the wooden block on a horizontal surface.
Attach a string to the block and connect it to a spring balance.
Pull the block gently and note the reading just when the block is about to move (marginal friction).
Add known weights on the block to increase normal reaction.
Repeat the experiment for different loads.
Record the corresponding values of marginal friction and normal reaction.
Plot a graph between frictional force (F) and normal reaction (R).
calculations: Calculate normal reaction R = total weight on the block.
Note marginal friction from spring balance readings.
Plot graph between F and R.
Determine coefficient of friction using μ = F / R or slope of graph.
precautions: Pull the block gently and horizontally.
Note the reading exactly at the point when motion just begins.
Ensure the surface is clean and dry.
Avoid jerks while pulling the block.
Keep the string parallel to the surface.
learning_outcome: To understand the dependence of friction on normal reaction and determine the coefficient of friction using experimental observations.

theory: A vector is a physical quantity that has both magnitude and direction. Vectors are represented graphically by arrows, where the length represents magnitude and the direction shows orientation. Vector addition can be performed using methods such as the head-to-tail method and parallelogram law. The resultant vector is obtained by combining two or more vectors and represents their net effect.

subject: Physics
experiment_name: Determination of Force Constant of a Spiral Spring
objective: To determine the force constant of a spiral spring by studying the relationship between applied weight and extension using a graph.
theory: When a force is applied to a spring, it undergoes extension. According to Hooke’s Law, the extension produced in a spring is directly proportional to the applied force, provided the elastic limit is not exceeded. Mathematically, F ∝ x or F = kx, where k is the force constant of the spring. A graph plotted between force (weight) and extension is a straight line passing through the origin, and its slope gives the force constant.
procedure: Suspend the spiral spring vertically from a rigid support.
Attach a weight hanger to the lower end of the spring.
Measure the initial length of the spring without any load.
Add a known weight and measure the new length of the spring.
Calculate the extension produced.
Repeat the experiment by adding different weights.
Record the corresponding extension for each weight.
Plot a graph between force (F) and extension (x).
calculations: Calculate force using F = mg for each load.
Determine extension (x = final length − initial length).
Plot graph between F and x.
Find slope of graph to determine force constant k.
precautions: Do not exceed the elastic limit of the spring.
Ensure the spring is hung vertically.
Take readings at eye level to avoid parallax error.
Add weights gently to avoid oscillations.
Measure lengths accurately.
sources_of_error: Spring not obeying Hooke’s law perfectly.
learning_outcome: To understand Hooke’s Law and determine the force constant of a spring using graphical analysis.

subject: Physics
experiment_name: Verification of Ohm's Law
objective: To verify Ohm’s Law by establishing the relationship between current and voltage for a given conductor and to determine the resistance of the conductor from the V-I graph.
theory: Ohm’s Law states that the current flowing through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across its ends, provided that temperature and other physical conditions remain constant. Thus, V ∝ I or V = IR, where R is the resistance of the conductor. Resistance depends on the nature, length, and cross-sectional area of the conductor. The V-I graph for an ohmic conductor is a straight line passing through the origin, and its slope represents the resistance.
procedure: Set up the circuit by connecting the battery, rheostat, ammeter, and resistor in series.
Connect the voltmeter in parallel across the resistor.
Check that all connections are tight and correct.
Close the key to allow current to flow.
Adjust the rheostat to obtain a small current reading.
Note the readings of ammeter (current) and voltmeter (voltage).
Vary the rheostat to change current and take 5–6 sets of readings.
Record all observations carefully.
Plot a graph between voltage (V) and current (I).
calculations: Calculate resistance using R = V / I for each reading.
Find the average resistance.
Determine resistance from slope of V-I graph (R = ΔV / ΔI).
precautions: Ensure all connections are tight and clean.
Ammeter must be connected in series and voltmeter in parallel.
Avoid heating of the resistor by keeping current low.
Take readings quickly to maintain constant temperature.
Check zero error before taking readings.
learning_outcome: To understand and verify the linear relationship between voltage and current and determine resistance using experimental data.

subject: Physics
experiment_name: Determination of Resistance of a Given Wire using Meter Bridge
objective: To determine the resistance of a given wire using a meter bridge and hence understand the working of a Wheatstone bridge.
theory: A meter bridge is a practical application of the Wheatstone bridge principle. It consists of a uniform wire of one meter length. When the bridge is balanced, no current flows through the galvanometer, and the ratio of resistances is equal to the ratio of lengths of the wire segments. If R is the known resistance and X is the unknown resistance, then at balance point, R/X = l/(100 − l), where l is the balancing length. This principle is used to determine the unknown resistance accurately. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}
procedure: Set up the meter bridge circuit with known resistance (R) in one gap and unknown resistance (X) in the other.
Connect the galvanometer between the central terminal and jockey.
Close the key to allow current to flow.
Move the jockey gently along the wire to find the point where galvanometer shows zero deflection (balance point).
Note the balancing length (l) from one end.
Repeat the experiment by changing the value of known resistance (R).
Record multiple readings and take the mean value.
Calculate the unknown resistance using the formula.
calculations: Note balancing length l for each observation.
Calculate unknown resistance using X = R (100 − l) / l.
Find the average value of resistance.
precautions: Ensure tight and clean connections.
Do not press the jockey too hard on the wire.
Avoid heating of the wire by keeping current low.
Take readings when galvanometer shows exact zero deflection.
Keep the balance point near the middle of the wire for accuracy.
sources_of_error: End error in meter bridge wire.
learning_outcome: To understand the working of Wheatstone bridge and accurately determine unknown resistance using a meter bridge.

subject: Physics
experiment_name: Determination of Internal Resistance of a Primary Cell using Potentiometer
objective: To determine the internal resistance of a given primary cell using a potentiometer.
theory: A potentiometer is a device used to measure potential difference accurately without drawing current from the source. The potential drop along a uniform wire is directly proportional to its length. When the circuit is open, the balancing length (l1) gives the emf of the cell. When the circuit is closed through a known resistance, the balancing length (l2) gives the terminal voltage. The internal resistance (r) of the cell is given by r = R[(l1 / l2) − 1], where R is the external resistance.
procedure: Set up the potentiometer circuit with a battery to maintain a steady current through the wire.
Connect the primary cell in the secondary circuit with a galvanometer and jockey.
Keep the key open and find the balancing length (l1) for emf.
Now close the key to include a known resistance in the circuit.
Find the new balancing length (l2) for terminal voltage.
Repeat the experiment with different values of resistance.
Record all readings carefully.
Calculate internal resistance using the formula.
calculations: Note balancing length l1 for emf.
Note balancing length l2 for terminal voltage.
Substitute values in r = R[(l1 / l2) − 1].
Find average internal resistance.
precautions: Ensure all connections are tight and clean.
Do not pass high current through the potentiometer wire.
Touch the wire lightly with jockey to avoid damage.
Ensure steady current throughout the experiment.
Take accurate readings of balancing lengths.
learning_outcome: To understand the working of a potentiometer and determine the internal resistance of a cell accurately.

subject: Physics
experiment_name: Determination of Resistance of a Galvanometer by Half-Deflection Method
objective: To determine the resistance of a given galvanometer using the half-deflection method.
theory: The half-deflection method is used to determine the resistance of a galvanometer. Initially, a current is passed through the galvanometer producing a certain deflection. A known resistance is then connected in parallel (shunt) so that the deflection reduces to half. At this condition, the shunt resistance is approximately equal to the resistance of the galvanometer. This is based on the principle of division of current in parallel circuits.
procedure: Connect the galvanometer in series with a battery and a high resistance box.
Adjust the resistance to obtain a suitable deflection in the galvanometer.
Note the initial deflection (θ).
Now connect a shunt resistance in parallel with the galvanometer.
Adjust the shunt resistance until the deflection becomes half (θ/2).
Note the value of shunt resistance.
Repeat the experiment for different initial deflections.
Calculate the resistance of the galvanometer.
calculations: Note initial deflection θ.
Adjust shunt resistance until deflection becomes θ/2.
Take shunt resistance value as galvanometer resistance (Rg ≈ S).
Find average value of galvanometer resistance.
precautions: Ensure proper and tight connections.
Do not pass excessive current through the galvanometer.
Adjust resistance to get a steady deflection.
Read deflection without parallax error.
Make fine adjustments for exact half deflection.
learning_outcome: To understand the principle of current division and determine the resistance of a galvanometer using the half-deflection method.
